The VIX last week saw its biggest weekly drop in percentage terms since December 2021. History says that bodes well for short-term returns and isn’t bad for longer-term ones, but less so when the VIX starts near 30 or higher, as it did this time.

There have been only 10 other weekly VIX drops of 30% or more since 1990. The S&P 500 was higher a week later in seven of them (median +0.6%) and a month later in eight (+1.6%), better on both counts than all weeks (higher 57% and 64% of the time, with median gains of 0.3% and 1.3%).

Three months later, though, it was higher in only six (+2.0%), trailing all weeks (71%, +3.2%). Six and 12 months out, it was higher in seven of 10 (+8.7%) and seven of nine (+15.5%), slightly worse odds than for all weeks (74% and 81%), but the median gains beat those for all weeks (+5.7% and +12.0%).

The cases most like this one, however, were weaker starting a month out. In the five that started from a VIX near 30 or higher, the S&P 500’s median return was +1.2% a week later but flat a month later. It was higher three months later in just two (median −0.7%), and the median gains six and 12 months out (+4.3% and +1.9%) trailed those for all weeks.

Their median worst close over the next three months was 4.2% below the drop-week close, vs. 2.3% for all 10 drops and 3.0% for all weeks. August 2007 and December 2021 came near major market tops, and after the latter the S&P 500 closed as much as 11.5% below its drop-week level within three months. It’s a small sample, but it argues for some caution beyond the near term.

After such an unusually large upgrade to GDP you might be asking "do those stick?".

Mostly, but usually not in full, and the closest precedent was later revised back to not far from where it started. 

Since 1985, there have been 16 quarters when the second estimate raised growth by 0.75 point or more. 

As of the most recent updates, growth in five of them is above even the second estimate, six landed between the advance and second estimates, and five fell below the advance estimate. 

On average, later revisions took back 0.25 point from the second estimate, or 0.51 point excluding the pandemic-distorted Q2 2020. 

The closest parallel, Q2 2015, the last bigger upgrade outside the pandemic, went from 2.32% to 3.68% and now stands at 2.50%. 

The worst outcomes came in Q3 2002 and Q3 2007, when growth ended about 1.5 points below even the advance estimate, at 1.64% and 2.32%. On the other side, Q2 1997 went from 2.16% to 3.62% and now stands at 6.83%.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
While not a "record," GDP revisions of the size we got Wednesday are, in fact, unusual. 

The 0.91-point upgrade was the largest from the advance to the second estimate since Q2 2020, and excluding the pandemic, the largest since Q2 2015, according to the Philadelphia Fed’s real-time data. 

Since 1985, the average advance-to-second revision has been 0.44 point in either direction. The print is also now a full point above the Atlanta Fed GDPNow model’s final Q3 reading of 3.27%.

Treasury yields rose Friday, with the 10-year up 7 basis points, snapping its eight-day losing streak (its longest since 2024).

Interestingly, history leans towards higher yields after such streaks in the next three months and more heavily in that direction longer term. 

After the 11 prior streaks of eight or more straight daily declines since 1962, the 10-year yield was higher a week later in six of them (median +3 basis points), a month later in seven (+4bp) and three months later in six (+3bp), modestly better than the roughly 50-50 odds for all days. 

A bigger difference came further out, with the yield higher six and 12 months later in eight of the 11 (73%) and median rises of 47bp and 20bp, compared with 3bp and 7bp for all days. 

The most recent, which ended August 5, 2024, at 3.78%, saw the yield rise 53bp over the next three months. It’s a small sample, though, with three of the 11 in 1970-71.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
BLACK FRIDAY WAS BORN IN PHILADELPHIA: In the 1950s and 1960s, the day after Thanksgiving brought absolute chaos to Center City. Shoppers packed Wanamaker's, Gimbels and Strawbridge & Clothier, while thousands of football fans descended on Philadelphia for the annual Army–Navy game.

The crowds and traffic became so overwhelming that Philadelphia police dubbed the day “Black Friday.” Local merchants tried to rebrand it as “Big Friday,” but the original name stuck. What started as a Philadelphia policing nightmare eventually became a nationwide shopping tradition. Just another piece of American culture that originated in Philly.

Who remembers Christmas shopping in Center City during its glory days?

🪙Lots of eyes on USD1 overnight after briefly depegging. Here is a look from @TheTerminal stablecoin dashboard: 

The supply chart is worth a look. Circulating supply is $2.72B, and the slide started well before last night:

• Supply last peaked near $4.47B on Oct. 6. It's down about $1.75B, or 39%, in under eight weeks.

• November has done most of the damage: roughly $1.15B gone this month, a 30% drop.

• After a week of holding steady around $2.85B, supply fell about $129M today (4.5%), the largest one-day decline in the past six months.

• From the June high of $4.85B, it's down 44%.

Burns are outpacing mints.

tweets.text:
Yesterday I released The 2027 Macro Outlook to MACROSHARK members.

This one was a labor of love. The result is 85 pages, more than 20,000 words and over 80 charts on where we are in the cycle, where liquidity goes next and how I think the year plays out.

People like to say macro is a puzzle. It most certainly is. You're trying to put the pieces together to see the complete picture.

But I think of it more like a Rubik's Cube. Solve one side and you can scramble another. Very rarely do all six sides line up at once. When they do, conditions are aligned for something good to happen.

I think 2027, much like 2026, will be a year of two halves. And the cube may end up showing all its sides at once... but that's more a story for the second half than the first.

I'm proud of it, and I hope members get as much out of reading it as I did out of writing it.
